Name: Wrodium
Notes William:
I don't see sustainability. As AI get's better, they hopefully will hallucinate less. I don't fully understand the product as they don't explain a lot and focus more on their traction.

Their traction is solid. They have consistent growth, pilot-users and paying customers. Their value is present through their statistics.

They published a paper, which might be an indication that this is more than just a AI wrapper. It seems to be a more deeptech-oriented company.

Even though I don't necessarily see this startup as sustainable, I do see exit potential. A lot of the public is worried about misinformation and publishers would want to be able to provide accurate information. I can see Wrodium being acquired by large publishers.

They are a pre-seed startup, and have already acquired multiple paying customers. It could prove a very beneficial investment.
Notes Wout: The long-term sustainability is questionable, as AI hallucinations will ideally decrease as models mature. The product itself is somewhat vague, with the pitch emphasizing traction over mechanics. However, that traction is undeniably solid, evidenced by steady growth, pilot programs, and paying clients. Their statistics show clear value. The publication of a research paper suggests a deep-tech foundation rather than a simple AI wrapper. Despite doubts about the business model's longevity, the exit strategy is clear. With rising concerns over misinformation, large publishers seeking accuracy tools might look to acquire Wrodium. Given they are pre-seed yet already generating revenue, this could be a high-potential investment.

Name: Scholé
Notes William:
Their idea makes sense, and the timing couldn't be better. The AI act in Europe forces companies to explain their AI usage to their employers, which is what Schole does exactly. Their USP, mainly being their exclusivity is what sets them apart. They have incredible connections and partners, which provides a great market advantage. 

The team isn't that strong, with both founders having a primary academic background.

Their use of the compliance deadline is very clever. Companies have until august 2026 to find a solution for this problem, and Schole is a convenient one.

Very promising startup, with a clear competitive advantage and value proposition.
Notes Wout: The concept is logical and the timing is impeccable. With the European AI Act requiring companies to disclose AI usage to employees, Schole addresses this exact need. Their primary differentiator is exclusivity, backed by strong partnerships and connections that offer a significant market edge. While the team is heavily academic and perhaps less experienced commercially, their strategy regarding the August 2026 compliance deadline is brilliant. Schole offers a convenient solution for that mandate. Overall, a highly promising venture with a distinct value proposition and competitive lead.

Notes William: The technology, idea, and patent are genuinely strong. Still, I’m not a fan of them relying solely on their own platform instead of integrating with the tools companies already use. Their TransferChain SDK is far more compelling, it actually fits into existing workflows and feels like the real product opportunity. The company has been active since 2019, which adds credibility, but by now you’d expect more visible traction and clearer adoption.
Competitors Wout: Apple (covers most core TransferChain Pass features through ecosystem integration), Google Workspace (offers similar identity and data-sync functionality across devices)
Notes Wout: Technology, idea and patent are really strong. Not a fan of them using their own platform to use it without any integration to existing platforms companies use. Their TransferChain SDK is way more interesting due to it being applicable in existing workflows. Company has already been active since 2019.

Currently lot of competitors so need to investigate how their technology stands up against competitors. No clear UPS. Having a CMO in the founding team for a product like this feels unnecessary and irrelevant.

Name: Promptlaw
Competitors William: Jurimesh (due diligence), Emma Legal (contract review), Spellbook (drafting), ContractPodAI (full AI lawyer)
Notes William: Technically, they seem to prioritize output accuracy, which is good. However, aiming for an "all-in-one" AI lawyer is risky compared to niche competitors like Emma Legal. The massive hurdle is liability: if the AI makes an error, they have no mechanism to take responsibility. Without that assurance, clients won't switch from human lawyers.
Competitors Wout: Jurimesh focusses on legal due diligence. Emma legal on reviewing contracts. Spellbook focussen on drafting contracts. ContractPodAI also offers a full AI lawyer not bound to a specific area.
Notes Wout: From a technical pov it looks like they know the importance of providing correct output. It does feel ambitious to not pick a more specific niche to focus on. For example Emma Legal is a startup focussing on reviewing contract. Jurimesh is a startup focussing on legal due dilligence. To be a all round AI lawyer is ambitious to start. On the other hand it does mean they can offer an all-in-one package to customers, which is really future proof. Only concern I have is that while they do have a lot of technical ways to minimize errors in output, they currently don't have a way to take responsibility in case of an error. This could lead to clients not wanting to switch to a full AI lawyer.

The sports market is undeniably large, but it seems like there is a real segmentation problem here. The users who would pay a premium for workout analysis are the ones who need precise, reliable readings, and those are exactly the people who are most likely to distrust a video-only approach. Meanwhile the more casual end of the market, who might actually be comfortable with video-based feedback, tend to care a lot less about in-depth analysis in the first place and are harder to monetize. That gap between who would pay and who the product actually works best for feels like a meaningful structural issue.

Notes Wout: When the analysis and feedback is fully based on video instead of real measuring tools, what is the tradeoff in accuracy?
